# Discrete Computational Models

In this section, we change the computational model. So far, each slot of a ciphertext has held an arbitrary complex number, and functions such as sign could only be approximated (recall the [disclaimer](/sign/discrete-math.qmd) in Discrete Math). Here, we instead assume our inputs come from a finite, discrete set, such as integers in a fixed range. The allowed moves from [Setup](/setup.qmd) stay the same; what changes is the kind of input we assume and how we store it in the slots.

In the case that our domain has finite discrete values, any function on that domain can be represented by a polynomial. Since there are a finite number of inputs, we can interpolate a polynomial that agrees with the function at every one of them.

For example, on the three-point set $\{-1, 0, 1\}$, the polynomial
$$
\frac{x^2 + x}{2}
$$

takes the values $0, 0, 1$ at $x = -1, 0, 1$ respectively. On this set, it agrees *exactly* with the indicator of $x > 0$. Unlike the sign approximations in Discrete Math, the polynomial only needs to be correct at the three allowed inputs, so it never has to jump: it just has to go from $0$ at $x = 0$ to $1$ at $x = 1$, a whole unit away (compare with the accuracy windows in [Sign Applicability](/sign/applicability.qmd)). CKKS arithmetic is still approximate, so the computed values will be close to $0$ or $1$ rather than exactly equal, with errors on the order of the precision from [Setup](/setup.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="**Remark**"}
Of course, this depends on the user supplying their data in a discrete form. Since users encrypt their own inputs, they can supply not only $x$ but also its binary digits or its root-of-unity form (much like supplying inverses in [Division](/division/intro.qmd)). The catch is that not every operation preserves this form: adding binary digits requires carrying, and multiplying numbers stored as roots of unity calls for a lookup table. So each choice of form makes certain things easier and other things harder.
:::

A finite domain may be encoded by integers modulo some fixed $n$. We explore two such encodings: roots of unity and $k$-bit binary. With this in mind, we discuss uses such as modular arithmetic, the sign function, and sorting, and consider the computational costs and numerical accuracy of these methods.
